Send that email. Be polite but firm. Something like "Could you please let us know specifically when you will be showing our unit so we can make sure we are available or at least prepared?" That is a completely reasonable request and you are not being an asshole for making it.

Also look into your state's tenant rights laws because what he is doing, especially walking into your bedrooms and getting angry when you lock your doors, may actually be illegal. Your bedroom is your private space and you have every right to lock it. The situation with your friend being woken up by him walking into her room while she was sleeping is particularly concerning and could be considered a violation of her rights as a tenant.

Document everything. Save every email he sends. Note the dates and times he shows up unannounced. If he is violating tenant rights laws, you want a paper trail.

Good luck with the family friend reviewing your lease. That is a smart move and I hope it gives you some clarity and leverage here.

NTA for moving the cart, but I think you handled the aftermath poorly.

Moving the cart was fine. It was a practical solution to a minor obstacle, and you weren't rude about it. She wasn't there, there was no purse on it, you moved it a foot. No big deal.

But when she made her comment about asking her to move it, that was actually a pretty reasonable thing to say. She had a point - asking would have been the more polite option, even if moving it yourself was also acceptable. At that point you could have just said "sorry about that" and moved on. Instead you got defensive and then told her not to leave her cart in the middle of the aisle, which was unnecessarily confrontational. She wasn't being aggressive with you, just mildly pointing something out.

So - NTA for the cart move itself, but a little bit YTA for escalating what could have been a nothing interaction into a minor confrontation. It was a busy holiday weekend in a packed Walmart. Everyone is a little frazzled. Sometimes the right move is to just let the small stuff go rather than needing to have the last word.

NTA, but I want to be clear - the issue isn't that you're telling them you didn't sign on for this, it's HOW and WHY you're having that conversation that matters.

You took in a friend in crisis, which was incredibly kind. Nobody signs on for four ER trips in a week, sleeping arrangements being completely upended, and the kind of mental and emotional drain you're all clearly experiencing. That's not what was agreed to, and it's okay to acknowledge that out loud.

But here's the thing - what's the goal of telling them this? If it's to set some boundaries around your own capacity and figure out a plan together, that's completely reasonable. If it's to make them feel guilty for being sick, that's where it gets complicated, because they're not choosing this either.

Some practical stuff worth thinking about:

Their medical team needs to be looped in on the fact that they don't have a stable support system that can sustain this level of care long term. Social workers exist for exactly this situation and can help connect them to resources.

You need to have a house meeting about sustainability. Not a blame session, but a real conversation about what you CAN offer going forward and what you can't.

You are allowed to be exhausted and resentful and scared. All of that is valid. You're also clearly good people for doing what you've done so far. Both things are true.

>I mentioned to a coworker that on the bright side it worked out for me so at least that's a positive.

Yeah, you read the room wrong here. Even if you genuinely feel that way, saying it out loud at a team lunch where people are visibly upset about someone they considered a friend is just... not it. That's not about being depressed over things you can't control, that's just basic social awareness.

You don't have to feel bad for her. You don't have to pretend to be sad. But there's a difference between not performing grief and actively pointing out that her misfortune is your gain while people around you are upset about it. Keep that thought to yourself next time.

Also worth noting - you don't actually know what happened. "Some people who know her friends said" is about as reliable as it gets, and H1B situations can be incredibly complicated, especially for people from countries like Syria where the immigration process is already a minefield. Not saying she's innocent, just that you're filling in a lot of blanks with assumptions about someone you already had a negative bias toward.

The coworker who got upset isn't wrong for being upset. You're not wrong for feeling the way you do internally. You're just wrong for saying it out loud in that moment.

That's not indifference, that reads as cruelty to them even if it wasn't intended that way.

The lesson here isn't to fake grief you don't feel. It's to understand that not every thought needs an audience and that choosing your moment is a basic social skill, especially in a workplace where you now need these people to respect you in a more senior role.

same2.text:
NTA and please go back.

Cemeteries have been public green spaces and places of quiet contemplation for centuries. The Victorians literally designed them that way on purpose - Père Lachaise in Paris, Highgate in London, Green-Wood in Brooklyn - these were built as parks for the living as much as resting places for the dead. People picnicked in them. Families spent Sunday afternoons walking the paths. It was considered healthy and appropriate.

Reading gravestones is one of the most quietly respectful things a person can do. You are acknowledging that these people existed. You are pausing in your day to register their names, their dates, sometimes their epitaphs. That is not disrespect. That is the opposite of being forgotten.

The person who confronted you was grieving and raw and projected their pain onto you. That is completely understandable and human. But their grief does not make you wrong. You were not loud, you were not littering, you were not intruding on their visit. You were sitting on a bench eating a sandwich.

I am also an introvert and I understand viscerally what you are describing - the need to find a quiet pocket in a loud day to simply *be*. A well-kept cemetery with shade trees and gravel paths and benches is exactly the kind of place that exists for that. The benches are not decorative. Someone put them there for people to sit on.

Go back. Be peaceful. Be respectful, which you already are. That is enough.

NTA and stop feeling bad.

Let's look at what you actually did: you offered $20 to a neighbour who has your screwdriver set, kept your ladder for weeks, used your internet for a month without a word about chipping in, and has a consistent pattern of taking without returning or reciprocating. You offered what you could afford. That's not stingy, that's sensible.

The cold shoulder and the 'stingy' comment to other neighbours is her trying to reframe this so she's the victim. Classic move. She's embarrassed and deflecting. Don't let her narrative take root.

Here's what I'd do. Go get your screwdriver set back. Today if possible, this week at the latest. Knock on her door, be pleasant, 'Hey Kyah, while I'm thinking of it can I grab my screwdriver set back?' Don't make it about the grocery store. Just reclaim your property calmly and matter of factly.

Going forward, the lending stops. Not because you're punishing her, but because you've learned something valuable about how she operates. She's not malicious, she's just one of those people who takes the path of least resistance and you've been that path. 

Let the other neighbour's opinion sort itself out over time. People who know you will see who she is eventually. People who don't know you well enough to form their own opinion don't matter yet.

You did nothing wrong here.

Should have addressed only the Mom? You did. Twice. She looked through you like you were a window. At some point you address whoever is actually capable of stopping the behavior, and that turned out to be nobody.

Should have yelled so the kid knew you were serious? Absolutely not. You spoke to a child calmly and clearly. That's correct. The fact that it didn't work is a parenting failure, not a delivery failure.

Your friend's instinct to move is the practical answer and yes, in hindsight, earlier is better. But you weren't wrong to hold your ground either.

"You're horrible" on the way out? Honestly, earned.

NTA. 

Oh this is a classic. You just opened a business, you have startup costs, you have supply costs, you have overhead and you have bills. And your 'friend' wants you to work for free. Let's be very clear about what she's asking - she wants you to spend money on supplies, spend your time and physical energy (massage is hard physical work, you only have so many sessions in your hands and body per day) and get nothing back. That's not friendship, that's exploitation with a smile on it.

'If you really cared you'd make it happen.' If SHE really cared she wouldn't ask you to jeopardize your brand new business before it's even found its feet. If the mutual friends really cared they'd be booking paid appointments to support you, not piling on because Diana is sulking.

Here's what I'd say to Diana: 'I offered you a significant discount as a friend. That's what friendship looks like in this context. What you're asking for is for me to pay to work on you, because my supplies aren't free. I won't do that for anyone right now, friend or not. When I'm established and profitable, we can revisit. Until then, the discount stands or we don't do this at all.'

And to the mutual friends: 'Cool, book an appointment then. Show me you support me.'

Your business, your rules. People who guilt you into working for free aren't your community, they're freeloaders.

Could you have responded more calmly? Sure, probably. But I think most people would have reacted similarly when someone invades your personal space and speaks to you condescendingly out of nowhere. You didn't start anything, you ignored his initial comment, and he escalated it by physically approaching you. The reaction he got was a direct result of his own behavior.

The fact that he then threatened to report YOU is almost laughable. Report you for what exactly? Telling him to back off after he harassed you?

YTA. You made not one, but TWO rude comments to your wife's co-worker (who was also your host) about her party choices. "Oh, I thought this was a party" was condescending and dismissive. Then when she asked if something was wrong with the drink, instead of just saying "no thanks, I'll grab some water," you told her you weren't interested in drinking "straight sugar." That's just unnecessarily rude. She didn't ask for your opinion on her beverages.

Nobody is obligated to serve alcohol at their party. Dry parties are a thing. Maybe she's in recovery, maybe she has religious reasons, maybe she just didn't want to deal with drunk co-workers at her house. None of that is your business. You were a guest.

You also knew going in that you wouldn't know anyone there. Instead of making the best of it and supporting your wife at her new job, you sulked, kept to yourself, and managed to insult the host twice. Your wife is rightfully embarrassed. Apologize to her and honestly, probably to the host too.

NTA, but you're also not totally blameless here.

The workers weren't wrong to close the doors at 8:59 - that's literally what the rules are and you knew that. And honestly, sending your wife to fill a water bottle at 8:59 when you hadn't even started boarding yet was a mistake. You should have been at your gate and ready to go, not at the neighboring gate and not filling water bottles when boarding was happening.

That said, the workers handled this pretty poorly. If your wife was standing right there at the door, the least they could do is say "ma'am, we're closing the doors right now" instead of just shutting it in front of her and then avoiding eye contact with you. That's just bad customer service and honestly a little cowardly.

The real kicker here is the 24-hour check-in thing. Good on you for catching that and pushing back, because that was a pretty transparent attempt to make your situation worse than it needed to be. The fact that she just... waited a few seconds and printed the passes anyway says a lot about how much of that was actually necessary versus just being unhelpful.

Bottom line: you cut it too close and paid the price, which is on you. But the workers weren't exactly going above and beyond to help a family with two small kids either.

Hope you get home soon.
